butchering-prepare-desc: Keep a sharp knife ready for skinning and prepare a hook and table before your next hunt. Flint tools and primitive workstations are enough to begin. Save a separate knife for working at the hook: the tools used to build a butchering table are consumed in its recipe.
butchering-hook-desc: Combine flint hook components with logs, sticks, flint and resin or fat using the handbook recipe. Place the skinning hook with room for a hanging carcass beneath it. Hang an intact corpse and hold right-click with a knife to skin it; a cleaver cannot do this work. The primitive hook has an 80% drop rate for the skinning stage. The animal and its condition determine the available products and quantities.
butchering-table-desc: Build a primitive butchering table with the handbook grid recipe. Its stone knife and axe are consumed, so keep another knife for skinning. Carry the table in a backpack equipment slot and place it like a filled skep, using Ctrl with the backpack-slot controls. Leave room for its three-block footprint extending two blocks to the right. Its 80% drop rate applies to the table-processing stage; the carcass determines which products are available.
butchering-retrieve-desc: Approach an unharvested animal corpse with an empty active hand and right-click to pick it up. A chicken, hare or fox makes a manageable first load and fits in ordinary inventory. Larger corpses need backpack equipment space. Carry the animal straight to your prepared hook: corpses slow you down and spoil. Cutting it up in the field sacrifices yield.
butchering-skin-desc: Hang a suitable mammal on the skinning hook and hold right-click with a knife. Collect its raw hide for leatherwork or hide glue, then leave the carcass hanging to bleed. Birds give feathers, and some animals give fur rather than a raw hide. Choose your animal according to the material you need.
butchering-bleed-desc: Place an empty wooden bucket beneath the hanging carcass before bleeding finishes. After skinning with a knife, leave the animal on the hook until it has bled out; it cannot be removed during bleeding. Small, medium and large workloads take more than one, two or four game hours respectively. Take down the finished carcass with an empty hand and bring it to the table. An inventory-sized animal is easiest to handle at first.
butchering-process-desc: Lay a bled-out carcass on the butchering table and hold right-click with a knife or cleaver until the work is finished. A cleaver spends less durability on this work. Gather the meat and other products promptly and move the food into storage or preservation. Species, weight and condition affect the yield; different animals supply different materials.
butchering-blood-desc: Set an empty wooden bucket beneath the hanging carcass before it finishes bleeding. Follow the Butchering guide for placement and check that blood reaches the bucket. Collect at least one whole litre and carry the filled container in your hotbar or backpack; a full bucket is unnecessary. Reserve some blood for sausage: a batch uses 0.2 litres.
butchering-preserve-desc: Choose a food whose handbook entry supports smoking and put it on the Butchering smoking rack with a firepit below. Ordinary raw meat is enough to start. Follow the rack's smoking instructions, collect the smoked food when ready, and store it before it spoils. Save whole Rustic Cookery slabs for their wooden smoke rack instead.
butchering-offal-desc: When table processing yields bloody offal, clean it in a barrel using its handbook recipe. Keep the clean offal for blood sausage or other suitable food recipes. Not every animal supplies offal, so make use of it when it appears among your butchering products.
butchering-sinew-desc: Set aside wet sinew from an animal that yields it and let it dry according to its handbook entry. Store the dry sinew for compatible bow and sewing recipes, or grind it for sinew glue. Keep it separate from fresh food while you prepare the rest of the carcass.
butchering-bones-desc: Some animals leave a bone carcass after table processing. Break it down and collect the available remains, including strong bones where the species supplies them. Check the strong bone's handbook recipes to choose a use for it. Ordinary bones can instead be ground into bonemeal.
butchering-bag-desc: Make a butchery bag to help bring animals home. Start with the primitive bag if you are still using stone tools. Compare the bag's capacity with the size of your intended prey before setting out, and equip it for the return trip. Prepare your workstations first so the carcass does not spend its freshness waiting for construction.
butchering-hunt-desc: Start with a chicken for an easier hunt; larger animals can fight back. Prepare a knife, skinning hook and butchering table before leaving home. Pick up the unharvested corpse with an empty active hand and bring it back for processing. Field cutting remains useful when you cannot carry the animal, but gives a reduced yield.
butchering-leather-desc: Turn raw hides into leather by preparing limewater, soaking and scraping the hides, then following the tanning recipes with weak and strong tannin. Use the linked leatherwork steps to prepare each barrel before committing your hides. Oiling a hide makes a pelt instead; keep hides intended for leather on the tanning route.
butchering-leather-links: Leatherwork: raw hide, limewater, hide soaking, hide scraping, hide preparation, leather tanning, weak tannin and strong tannin.
butchering-iw-links: Use bark from Immersive Woodworking board cutting in suitable tannin recipes. Check the barrel recipe for the bark it accepts.
butchering-tailor-links: Prepare an awl and a needle for Tailor's Delight sewing, then choose a hide bundle or finished-goods recipe from the handbook.
butchering-hunt-link: Before setting out, prepare your knife and processing area.
butchering-bh-link: Plan your Better Husbandry breeding stock before choosing animals for slaughter. Keep enough healthy breeding animals for the next generation.
butchering-lw-link: Prepare feeding troughs and maintain your breeding stock when raising animals with Livestock Welfare. Choose surplus animals for the butchering shed.
butchering-native-guides: Consult the Butchering guide for workstation use and the species and yields guide when choosing prey. Click a workstation or product icon to open its handbook page.
butchering-ef-rack-link: For another way to preserve meat, use the Expanded Foods meat rack and follow its dry-aging instructions.
butchering-chef-salt-link: Prepare salt for salting recipes with Chef's Tricks salt crystallization and salt-crystal drying.
butchering-ef-sausage-link: Use suitable ingredients in Expanded Foods sausage preparation. Check the recipe before setting aside meat or offal.
butchering-bonemeal-link: Put ordinary bones to use by grinding bonemeal; save strong bones for their own recipes.
butchering-cleaver-link: Prepare a cleaver for table work and keep a knife for skinning at the hook.
butchering-knapped-hook-desc: Knap flint using the hook pattern to make two hook components. Combine them with the other ingredients in the primitive skinning-hook recipe. The assembled primitive station has an 80% drop rate for skinning; the loose components are building materials, not workstations.
butchering-raw-slab-desc: Process suitable redmeat or bushmeat carcasses at the butchering table to gather Rustic Cookery slabs. Each complete group of six meat pieces forms a whole slab; smaller yields can leave ordinary meat instead. Keep a whole slab for smoking. To portion one, place it down and hold right-click with a knife or use a cleaver to cut pieces from it.
butchering-rustic-rack-desc: Build the wooden smoke rack with logs in the two upper corners and sticks in every remaining cell: LSL/SSS/SSS. Place it where smoke can reach the food and keep whole raw meat slabs ready. This rack handles Rustic Cookery slabs; use the separate Butchering smoking rack for its supported foods.
butchering-smoked-slab-desc: Right-click the Rustic Cookery smoke rack with a whole raw meat slab; partial slabs do not fit. Supply smoke from a fire using Real Smoke and watch the rack until the slab is fully smoked. Smoking progresses according to the smoke reaching the rack and pauses without it, rather than finishing after a fixed time. Collect and store the finished slab.
butchering-blood-sausage-desc: Arrange clean offal above a wooden bucket holding at least 0.2 litres of blood, with two raw or cured redmeat beneath it, in the crafting grid. Four raw or cured bushmeat, or three raw poultry, can replace the redmeat. The bucket is retained. Cook or smoke the raw blood sausage before eating it. Keep at least a whole litre of collected blood on hand when preparing your blood supply.
butchering-hide-glue-desc: Cook one litre of water with three scraped small hides or three scraped medium hides in a cooking pot. Collect at least one whole litre of hide glue in a container and carry it in your hotbar or backpack. Hot hide glue hardens into cold glue; reheat cold hide glue when you need it hot again. Keep spare prepared hides for leatherwork.
butchering-sinew-glue-desc: Grind dry sinew, then cook three ground sinew with one litre of water in a cooking pot to make cold sinew glue. Collect at least one whole litre in a container and carry it in your hotbar or backpack. Use sinew from animals that supply it, and reserve any dry lengths you need for sewing or bow recipes before grinding the rest.
butchering-metal-hook-desc: Smith a copper ingot with the four-hook anvil pattern to make four copper butchering hook components. Set them aside for a copper skinning hook or a suitable smoking-rack recipe. The assembled copper skinning station has a 100% drop rate for its skinning stage; the loose component has no processing rate of its own.
butchering-smoking-rack-desc: Arrange hook components, planks, sticks and resin in the grid pattern HPH/SRS/HPH. Use copper or bronze hooks for the copper rack recipe, or iron hooks for the iron rack. Set up a firepit below the rack and select foods with suitable smoking recipes. Keep whole Rustic Cookery slabs for their wooden smoke rack.
butchering-simple-table-desc: Prepare a copper or bronze knife, shears and cleaver, two copper plates and 32 planks. Assemble the simple table with its handbook grid recipe; the tools are consumed along with the plates and planks. Leave room for the table's full footprint when placing it. Its 100% drop rate applies to table processing, with products and quantities still depending on the carcass.
butchering-advanced-table-desc: Prepare an iron knife, shears and cleaver, two iron plates and 32 planks for the advanced table's handbook grid recipe. The tools are consumed in construction, so reserve working tools for the processing area. This table has a 120% drop rate for the table-processing stage. The rate improves that stage's yield; it does not promise a fixed quantity or every possible product from an animal.
butchering-prime-desc: Watch for prime cuts while processing eligible animals at the table. Set a raw prime cut aside for a recipe that makes good use of it, or preserve it before it spoils. Species and carcass condition affect what you receive; ordinary meat remains useful when a carcass supplies no prime cut.
butchering-bronze-component-desc: Smith a tin bronze, bismuth bronze or black bronze ingot with the four-hook anvil pattern to make four matching butchering hook components. Use them to assemble a bronze skinning hook or in a compatible smoking-rack recipe. The assembled bronze skinning station has a 100% drop rate for skinning; components alone do not process a carcass.
butchering-iron-component-desc: Work an iron ingot with the four-hook anvil pattern to make four iron butchering hook components. Save them for an iron skinning hook or iron smoking rack. The assembled iron skinning station has a 120% drop rate for its skinning stage; the loose hook is a construction component.
butchering-copper-skinning-hook-desc: Assemble the copper skinning-hook station with copper butchering hook components and the remaining handbook ingredients. Place it with room for a carcass and a wooden blood bucket below. Skin with a knife, then let the animal bleed. Its 100% drop rate applies to skinning yield, not a fixed number of products from every animal.
butchering-bronze-skinning-hook-desc: Build a bronze skinning-hook station using tin bronze, bismuth bronze or black bronze hook components in the corresponding handbook recipe. Leave room beneath it for a carcass and blood bucket. Use a knife for skinning. All three bronze stations have a 100% drop rate for that stage; the animal determines the products available.
butchering-iron-skinning-hook-desc: Assemble the iron skinning-hook station using iron butchering hook components and the handbook recipe. Prepare the wooden blood bucket before skinning the hanging animal with a knife. The iron station has a 120% drop rate for the skinning stage, improving its yield without guaranteeing a particular product or quantity.
butchering-copper-ceiling-hook-desc: Combine a complete copper floor-standing skinning-hook block with a wrench in the crafting grid to convert it to a ceiling hook. Mount it overhead with space for the hanging carcass and blood bucket. Reverse the conversion with the wrench when you need a floor-standing station again. The skinning-stage drop rate remains 100% in either form.
butchering-bronze-ceiling-hook-desc: Use the crafting grid to combine a complete bronze floor-standing skinning-hook block with a wrench. The ceiling form frees floor space while keeping room below for the animal and its blood bucket. Convert it back with the wrench when rearranging your shed. Tin bronze, bismuth bronze and black bronze retain their 100% skinning-stage drop rate in either form.
butchering-iron-ceiling-hook-desc: Convert a complete iron floor-standing skinning-hook block into its ceiling form by combining it with a wrench in the crafting grid. Mount the station overhead and leave space below for a carcass and wooden bucket. The wrench also converts it back to its floor-standing form. Both forms retain the iron station's 120% skinning-stage drop rate.
butchering-copper-age-links: Prepare for copper hook smithing with first smithing.
butchering-bronze-age-links: Choose a hook alloy: tin bronze, bismuth bronze or black bronze.
butchering-iron-age-links: Prepare iron for hooks and table tools with iron smithing.
